Why does almost every society on
Earth treat eating another human
being as unthinkable?
We usually answer with morality,
religion, or simple disgust.
But what if the taboo has a
second root, one that runs through biology?
Today we follow the science:
a deadly brain disease,
a strange kind of infectious
protein, some uncomfortable
arithmetic, and the question of
whether evolution wrote a warning
into our bodies.
Our story begins in the 1950s,
in the eastern highlands of Papua New Guinea.
The Fore people lived there,
in remote mountain valleys that
outsiders had barely reached.
A baffling illness was taking their lives.
People stumbled, shook, and lost
control of their own bodies.
The Fore called it kuru,
a word that means shaking or trembling.
Outsiders later gave it a darker
nickname: the laughing death.
Patients first became unsteady
on their feet.
Then came tremors, slurred speech,
and sudden bursts of laughter they
could not control.
Within months to a couple of years,
they could no longer sit,
swallow, or speak.
Kuru was always fatal.
In 1957, a medical officer named
Vincent Zigas reported the strange
disease to a young American
physician, Carleton Gajdusek.
Together, they started asking the
obvious question.
What kind of illness was this?
It did not look like influenza,
malaria, or any known infection.
There was no fever.
There was no sign of bacteria.
And the pattern was truly strange:
kuru struck women and children
far more often than adult men.
Eventually the investigators looked
at funeral customs.
In the Fore community,
as in some other societies,
relatives of the dead sometimes
performed mortuary cannibalism.
Anthropologists who studied the
practice describe it as an act
of mourning and respect,
a way to keep the dead within
the family instead of leaving them
to the earth.
It was not hunger,
and it was not violence.
It was grief.
According to those accounts,
the body was shared by custom.
Men often received the muscle.
Women and children were more likely
to handle and eat other tissues,
including the brain.
And the brain, as it turned out,
was where the danger was concentrated.
A ritual born out of love had
become a path for a disease to
travel from one person to the next.
When pathologists looked at the
brains of kuru victims under a
microscope, they saw something
that looked almost impossible.
The tissue was full of tiny holes.
Neurons had died, and the brain
had taken on the look of a sponge.
Doctors now call this pattern
spongiform change.
And a researcher named William
Hadlow noticed in 1959 that it
resembled scrapie, a disease of sheep.
That was an early clue.
In the 1960s, Gajdusek's team tested the idea.
They injected brain tissue from
kuru victims into chimpanzees.
After a long wait,
the animals developed the same disease.
Kuru was infectious.
But the agent behind it survived
treatments that destroy ordinary
germs, and it took years to show itself.
For this work, Gajdusek would share
a Nobel Prize in 1976.
So what was the infectious agent?
For a long time, nobody knew.
In the early 1980s,
the neurologist Stanley Prusiner
proposed an answer that many
scientists found hard to believe.
The agent, he said,
might be made of protein alone,
with no genes of its own.
He gave it a name: the prion.
Prusiner received the Nobel Prize
in 1997, as the evidence for his
idea grew stronger.
Here is how it works.
Your brain makes a normal protein
called PrP, which folds into a specific shape.
A prion is the same protein,
folded the wrong way.
Imagine a key that has been bent.
The strange part is that a misfolded
protein can push a normal one into
the same bent shape.
And then that one bends the next.
The chain reaction spreads slowly,
nerve cell by nerve cell.
As the misfolded proteins pile
up, brain cells die,
and the tissue starts to break down.
Prions resist the enzymes that
normally clear away damaged proteins.
That is part of why the damage
cannot be stopped once it begins.
There is no cure for kuru or
for the other prion diseases.
They are always fatal.
Now comes the question many people ask.
Could you simply cook the meat
and make it safe?
For ordinary germs, cooking works.
Salmonella and E.
coli are destroyed by normal cooking
temperatures, because heat unravels
their proteins.
But prions are different.
Normal cooking does not reliably
inactivate them.
They can survive the chemicals
used to preserve tissue,
such as formaldehyde.
And a standard hospital sterilizing
cycle is not enough for prions,
which is why hospitals use harsher
protocols after surgery on a patient
with a prion disease.
How extreme is this resistance?
In a famous laboratory study from
the year 2000, a team led by
Paul Brown heated infected hamster
brain to six hundred degrees Celsius.
A small amount of infectivity still survived.
It did not survive at one thousand degrees.
That is a single lab experiment
on one strain of hamster scrapie,
but it shows how stubborn prions can be.
Your immune system also struggles here.
Normally, your body spots invaders
by the foreign proteins on their surface.
But a prion is built from a
protein your own body makes.
So the immune system mounts no
useful defense: no antibody
response, no fever, and no early warning.
The infection can travel along
nerves toward the brain,
while you feel completely well.
And it can wait for a very long time.
Kuru has one of the longest
incubation periods ever documented.
A study of the last kuru patients,
published in 2006, found that some
became ill roughly forty years
after exposure, and the researchers
concluded that the delay could
exceed fifty years.
Imagine being healthy for half
a century, with a hidden infection
that is already inside you.
One more point matters,
and it is important to be accurate.
Eating a person is not automatically
a prion infection.
The risk exists when the person
had a prion disease.
Kuru itself probably began with
a rare, spontaneous prion illness
in one person, and the funeral
meals then passed it along.
But because the danger is invisible
and the delay is so long,
nobody could safely tell the
difference at the time.
The world saw a related warning
in Britain in the 1980s and 1990s.
Cattle there were fed meat-and-bone
meal made from the remains of other
animals, which let a prion disease
spread through the herd.
The disease was called bovine
spongiform encephalopathy, or mad cow disease.
In 1996, a human form linked to
it, variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob
disease, was reported.
The lesson was clear:
feeding animals to their own species
is dangerous.
Prions are only the first reason.
A second comes from ecology.
Scientists call it biomagnification.
Some pollutants do not break down
easily, so they build up in living bodies.
The higher a creature sits in a
food chain, the more of them it
tends to carry.
Mercury, certain pesticides, and
other persistent chemicals collect
in the tissues of top predators
like sharks, and in people.
Humans eat across many levels of
the food chain, and we live a long time.
Our fat holds on to certain chemicals.
Our liver and kidneys can store
metals like cadmium.
Our bones can hold lead.
So the body of an adult human
carries a record of what that person
ate, drank, and breathed for decades.
Now consider a third protection,
one that works for you every day:
the species barrier.
When you eat beef,
chicken, or pork, most of the
microbes in that meat are adapted
to cows, chickens, or pigs.
Their molecular keys do not fit
the locks on your cells.
Most of them cannot take hold in you.
Cooking destroys many of the rest.
That distance between species is
a very real shield.
The barrier shrinks when the food
is a person.
A pathogen that already infects
humans is already tuned to human cells.
Hepatitis viruses, for example,
are adapted to people.
And during outbreaks of Ebola,
funerals where mourners handle
the body have helped to spread the virus.
To be fair, cooking destroys most
viruses and bacteria, so the real
danger is limited to what survives.
But prions do survive.
Did prehistoric people ever eat
each other simply to survive?
In 2017, the archaeologist James
Cole of the University of Brighton
tested that idea in the journal
Scientific Reports.
His approach was to calculate what
a human body is actually worth in calories.
Cole used the numbers for an adult
man weighing about sixty-six kilograms.
He estimated roughly one hundred
and forty-four thousand calories
for the whole body.
The parts people would normally
eat add up to about one hundred
and twenty-six thousand.
The skeletal muscle, the actual
meat, is only about thirty-two
thousand of those.
The heart offers about six hundred
and fifty calories, the kidneys
about three hundred and eighty,
and the brain and nerves about
two thousand seven hundred.
Now compare that with the animals
prehistoric hunters pursued.
Cole estimated that the muscle
of a mammoth holds about three
point six million calories.
A woolly rhinoceros holds about
one point two six million.
Even a red deer holds about one
hundred and sixty-four thousand,
several times more than a single
person's muscle.
Cole's own comparison makes the point.
If a group of twenty-five adults
had only a human body to eat,
the muscle would last about half a day.
A mammoth could feed the same group
for about two months.
So cannibalism was a poor deal
as a food source.
And this is exactly what Cole concluded.
The low food value,
he said, supports explanations
that are social or cultural,
not purely nutritional.
That does not mean prehistoric
cannibalism never happened.
Archaeologists have found cut-marked
human bones at many ancient sites.
Hunting a person is also far riskier
than hunting a deer,
since people fight back.
That is common-sense inference,
not a measured result.
But the calories, the danger,
and the disease risk all point
the same way.
Now let us turn to the feeling
itself: disgust.
We tend to treat it as a
purely mental reaction.
But many researchers think disgust
works like a behavioral immune system.
It pushes you away from things
that carry disease, such as rotten
food, waste, and sickness.
Brain imaging studies have found
that the insula, a region deep
in the brain, becomes active when
people feel disgust.
So the shudder you feel at certain
thoughts is not random.
It may be doing a job.
Here is a thought experiment,
and to be clear,
it is an imagined scenario,
not a record of real people.
Picture two groups of early humans.
Group A has no strong aversion
to eating their dead.
Group B feels an overwhelming revulsion.
Over many generations, which group
would you expect to suffer more
from prion disease and infection?
Group A, in this story,
would be hit harder.
Group B would stay healthier.
And that difference could,
over time, favor a stronger aversion.
There is another benefit.
A group that refuses to treat its
members as food can build stronger trust.
People who see each other as allies,
not as emergency rations,
can hunt together and raise children together.
So disgust, empathy, and taboo
may have reinforced one another.
We cannot prove that sequence.
But it is a reasonable hypothesis,
and scientists are still debating it.
Genetics adds one more intriguing clue.
In 2003, a team led by the
researcher Simon Mead studied a
gene called PRNP, which makes the
prion protein.
At position 129 of that protein,
people carry either of two versions.
Those with one copy of each version,
called heterozygotes, seemed to
be better protected.
Among Fore women who had survived
kuru, the majority were heterozygous.
The team then looked at populations
all over the world.
They found that the two versions
are common in many regions,
and they argued that this balance
may reflect natural selection.
Their suggestion was that deadly
prion epidemics, similar to kuru,
may have struck human populations
in the distant past.
This is an interpretation,
not a proven fact,
and later researchers have
challenged parts of the statistical method.
So treat it as a fascinating possibility.
Now back to Papua New Guinea.
In the late 1950s,
authorities and community leaders
worked to end mortuary feasting
among the Fore.
The ritual faded away.
In the years after,
kuru cases dropped.
Researchers later reported that
no one born after the practice
ended developed the disease.
The last known cases died in the
2000s, decades after the final funeral feast.
That is the long shadow of a long incubation.
Kuru showed medicine that an
infection can be carried by a protein alone.
It led to a Nobel Prize for
Gajdusek and, later, one for Prusiner.
And it helped scientists understand
diseases like mad cow disease and
other prion disorders, which are
still deadly today.
Prions, pollutants, the species
barrier, and a poor calorie return
all point the same way.
The taboo is also cultural,
and cultures differ.
But beneath the stories we tell,
there may be a quiet biological logic.
So the next time you meet
cannibalism in a horror film or
an old myth, remember that the
scariest part may not be the monster.
It may be something far smaller:
a single misfolded protein,
patient and invisible, bending
its neighbors one by one.
Nature does not always warn us loudly.
Sometimes the warning is a shudder.
